claim: Long non-coding RNA and small non-coding RNA were significantly altered in sepsis relative to health.
source: Via next-generation microarray analysis of leukocyte RNA we found that long non-coding RNA and, to a lesser extent, small non-coding RNA were significantly altered in sepsis relative to health.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states findings from microarray analysis showing alterations in non-coding RNA in sepsis patients compared to healthy subjects.

claim: Long non-coding RNA expression was largely recapitulated in human endotoxemia.
source: Long non-coding RNA expression, but not small non-coding RNA, was largely recapitulated in human endotoxemia.
evidence: The abstract states that long non-coding RNA expression patterns in sepsis were reproduced in the human endotoxemia model.

claim: Small non-coding RNA expression was not recapitulated in human endotoxemia.
source: Long non-coding RNA expression, but not small non-coding RNA, was largely recapitulated in human endotoxemia.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that small non-coding RNA patterns were not reproduced in human endotoxemia.

claim: Integrating RNA profiles and plasma protein levels revealed non-sensory olfactory receptor activity pathways.
source: Integrating RNA profiles and plasma protein levels revealed known as well as previously unobserved pathways, including non-sensory olfactory receptor activity.
evidence: The abstract states that integration of RNA and protein data revealed olfactory receptor activity as a pathway.

claim: 2–5 million deaths worldwide are attributable to sepsis.
source: It is estimated that 2–5 million deaths worldwide are attributable to sepsis (Fleischmann et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Fleischmann et al., 2016.

claim: Sepsis was recognized as a global health priority in 2017 by the World Health Assembly and WHO.
source: As such, sepsis has been recognized as a global health priority in 2017 by the World Health Assembly and WHO (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2017.

claim: No specific treatment for sepsis has been approved despite more than 100 clinical trials.
source: In spite of more than 100 clinical trials having evaluated drugs targeting specific components of the host response to infection (Marshall, 2014), no specific treatment for sepsis has been approved (Angus and van der Poll, 2013; Cecconi et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Marshall, 2014; Angus and van der Poll, 2013; and Cecconi et al., 2018.

claim: Protein-coding RNA expression profiling has helped broaden understanding of sepsis immunopathology.
source: Protein-coding RNA expression profiling of blood leukocytes from sepsis patients has helped to broaden our understanding of sepsis immunopathology (van der Poll et al., 2017), for example, by unmasking defects in leukocyte energy metabolism of sepsis patients (Cheng et al., 2016), and by classifying sepsis patients as transcriptomic endotypes with prognostic and pathophysiological value (Scicluna et al., 2017; Davenport et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2009).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations including van der Poll et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2016; Scicluna et al., 2017; Davenport et al., 2016; and Wong et al., 2009.

claim: The protein-coding part of genomes from different species is remarkably similar in numbers and functions.
source: From fruit flies to man, the protein-coding part of genomes from different species is remarkably similar in numbers and functions (Liu et al., 2013), which suggests that numerous aspects of complex biology in eukaryotes might stem from non-protein-coding regions of the genome.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: Non-coding RNAs were under negative evolutionary selection, implying functionality rather than transcriptional noise.
source: Moreover, such studies facilitated the demonstration that non-coding RNAs were under negative evolutionary selection, which implied functionality rather than plain 'transcriptional noise' (Ponjavic et al., 2007).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Ponjavic et al., 2007.

claim: A substantial proportion of non-coding RNA yields clear phenotypic effects in both in vitro and in vivo functional studies.
source: Indeed, a substantial proportion of non-coding RNA, by general convention defined as long (>200 nucleotides) or small (<200 nucleotides) non-coding RNAs, yields clear phenotypic effects in both in vitro and in vivo functional studies (Zhu et al., 2016; Gebert and MacRae, 2019; Atianand et al., 2016; Carpenter et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2016; Gebert and MacRae, 2019; Atianand et al., 2016; and Carpenter et al., 2013.

claim: Non-coding RNAs have been linked to human diseases.
source: Ever-growing numbers of small non-coding RNAs, for example micro (mi)RNAs (20–24 nucleotides), or long non-coding RNAs such as long intergenic non-coding (linc)RNAs, have been linked to human diseases (Bao et al., 2019; Esteller, 2011).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2019 and Esteller, 2011.

claim: Non-coding RNAs have capacity for precise regulation of cellular biological processes via epigenetic mechanisms.
source: An important aspect of non-coding RNAs is their capacity for precise regulation of cellular biological processes via epigenetic mechanisms, including complex immune system processes (Carpenter, 2018; Atianand and Fitzgerald, 2014; Mehta and Baltimore, 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Carpenter, 2018; Atianand and Fitzgerald, 2014; and Mehta and Baltimore, 2016.

claim: Principal component analysis showed clear partitioning of sepsis patients distinct from healthy subjects for protein-coding and long non-coding RNAs.
source: Principal component (PC) analysis of the most abundant protein-coding RNAs (n = 18,063) and long non-coding RNAs (n = 16,087) showed clear partitioning of patients with sepsis distinct from healthy subjects (Figure 1A).
evidence: The statement is supported by data from principal component analysis and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Small non-coding RNAs showed only minimal separation between patients and healthy subjects in principal component analysis.
source: In contrast, small non-coding RNAs (n = 4949) showed only minimal separation between patients and healthy subjects.
evidence: The statement is based on principal component analysis results comparing sepsis patients to healthy subjects.

claim: Long non-coding RNA transcripts exhibited the broadest expression perturbations in healthy participants and sepsis patients.
source: Notably, long non-coding RNA transcripts exhibited the broadest expression perturbations in healthy participants and sepsis patients, exemplified by the highest overall MDTH indices (Figure 1B).
evidence: The statement is supported by MDTH index data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: 15,097 protein-coding RNAs were significantly altered between sepsis patients and healthy subjects.
source: Comparing sepsis patients to healthy subjects identified 15,097, 13,158, and 635 significantly altered (adjusted p-value <0.01) protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNAs, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis with statistical significance threshold and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: 13,158 long non-coding RNAs were significantly altered between sepsis patients and healthy subjects.
source: Comparing sepsis patients to healthy subjects identified 15,097, 13,158, and 635 significantly altered (adjusted p-value <0.01) protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNAs, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis with statistical significance threshold and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: 635 small non-coding RNAs were significantly altered between sepsis patients and healthy subjects.
source: Comparing sepsis patients to healthy subjects identified 15,097, 13,158, and 635 significantly altered (adjusted p-value <0.01) protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNAs, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis with statistical significance threshold and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: LincRNAs, antisense, and pseudogene RNA transcripts represented the most highly altered long non-coding RNA biotypes in sepsis relative to health.
source: LincRNAs, antisense, and pseudogene RNA transcripts represented the most highly altered long non-coding RNA biotypes in sepsis relative to health (Figure 1D).
evidence: The statement is based on analysis of long non-coding RNA biotypes and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Micro (mi)RNAs, stem loop RNAs, and small nucleolar (sno)RNAs were the most abundant small non-coding RNA biotypes.
source: Micro (mi)RNAs, stem loop RNAs, and small nucleolar (sno)RNAs were the most abundant small non-coding RNA biotypes (Figure 1E).
evidence: The statement is based on analysis of small non-coding RNA biotypes and reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Gender and age of healthy subjects explained 5%, 4%, and 4% of the variation in protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNA expression, respectively.
source: Using a variance partition (multivariable) approach (Hoffman and Schadt, 2016), differences in gender and age of healthy subjects explained 5%, 4%, and 4% of the variation in protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNA expression, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The statement is based on variance partition analysis and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Demographics and clinical characteristics cumulatively explained 18%, 13%, and 8% of protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNA expression variance in sepsis patients, respectively.
source: In sepsis patients, a multivariable model that incorporated demographics and common clinical characteristics, including APACHE IV, SOFA scores, shock and Charlson comorbidity indices, cumulatively explained 18%, 13%, and 8% of protein-coding, long non-coding, and small non-coding RNA expression variance, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: The statement is based on multivariable variance partition analysis and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Sepsis primary site of infection and place of acquisition explained the highest proportion of variation in protein-coding (6.7%) and long non-coding (4.4%) RNA expression.
source: Specifically, sepsis primary site of infection (lung or abdomen) and place of acquisition (community or hospital) explained the highest proportion of variation in protein-coding (6.7%) and long non-coding (4.4%) RNA expression (Figure 2A).
evidence: The statement is based on variance partition analysis and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: 837 protein-coding RNAs and 80 long non-coding RNAs were significantly altered when comparing patients with septic shock to patients without shock.
source: Septic shock explained low proportions of variation in RNA expression (Figure 2A), and directly comparing patients with septic shock to patients without shock resulted in 837 and 80 significantly altered protein-coding and long non-coding RNA, respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis comparing shock vs. no shock patients and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: 146 significantly altered protein-coding RNAs were identified when evaluating RNA expression in patients discordant for survival after 28 days.
source: Evaluating RNA expression in patients discordant for survival after 28 days identified 146 significantly altered protein-coding RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis comparing survivors vs. non-survivors and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No significant differences were uncovered in non-coding RNA expression profiles between survivors and non-survivors.
source: No significant differences were uncovered in non-coding RNA expression profiles, suggesting that non-coding RNA profiles obtained on ICU admission may not be suitable as mortality predictors.
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis comparing survivors vs. non-survivors.

claim: Non-coding RNA profiles obtained on ICU admission may not be suitable as mortality predictors.
source: No significant differences were uncovered in non-coding RNA expression profiles, suggesting that non-coding RNA profiles obtained on ICU admission may not be suitable as mortality predictors.
evidence: The statement is an inference based on the lack of significant differences in non-coding RNA between survivors and non-survivors.

claim: 2361, 5053, 2925, and 43 significant differences in long non-coding RNA expression were found after 2, 4, 6, and 24 hr endotoxemia, respectively.
source: Long non-coding RNA expression was robustly altered in endotoxemia, with 2361, 5053, 2925, and 43 significant differences after 2, 4, 6, and 24 hr endotoxemia, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The statement is based on differential expression analysis at multiple time points in human endotoxemia and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The highest correlation coefficient (r2 = 0.51) for long non-coding RNA fold expression was found between sepsis and 4 hr post-LPS.
source: Comparing fold expression in sepsis (relative to health) to human endotoxemia revealed significant correlations after 2, 4, and 6 hr of endotoxemia (Figure 3D). The highest r2 was found for sepsis and 4 hr post-LPS (r2 = 0.51).
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis between sepsis and endotoxemia time points and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Correlation analysis of small RNA fold expression during endotoxemia against fold expression in sepsis revealed indirect correlations.
source: Correlation analysis of small RNA fold expression during endotoxemia against fold expression in sepsis revealed indirect correlations (Figure 3E).
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Hierarchical clustering uncovered 23 network modules each harboring more than 100 inter-correlating RNA transcripts.
source: Hierarchical clustering uncovered 23 network modules (clusters) each harboring more than 100 inter-correlating RNA transcripts (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The statement is based on weighted network analysis and hierarchical clustering with reference to Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Eight modules in the co-expression network were significantly enriched for long non-coding RNA relative to protein-coding RNA.
source: Eight modules in the co-expression network were significantly enriched for long non-coding RNA relative to protein-coding RNA (Fisher's adjusted p<0.01; Figure 4B).
evidence: The statement is based on enrichment analysis with statistical significance and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: 34% of non-coding RNA modules were organized into distinct units.
source: This suggests that the leukocyte long non-coding transcriptome of sepsis patients is primarily co-expressed with protein-coding RNA, but 34% of non-coding RNA modules were organized into distinct units.
evidence: The statement is an inference based on the enrichment analysis showing 8 out of modules enriched for long non-coding RNA.

claim: 49 small RNAs in five network modules had explained variance estimated >20%.
source: Considering miRNA profiles that were significantly altered in sepsis patients relative to health (Figure 1C), and miRNA-to-gene interactions (miRWalk method), we detected 49 small RNAs in five network modules with explained variance estimated >20%, including hsa-miR-200c-3p (translation initiation module), SNORD84 (regulation of cytokine secretion/Toll-like receptor [TLR] signaling module), HBII-276 (translation initiation module), hsa-miR-1275 (sensory perception of chemical stimulus/olfactory receptor activity module), and hsa-miR-664b-3p (neutrophil degranulation/extracellular exosome module) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The statement is based on integration of miRNA profiles with network modules and reference to Figure 4E.

claim: hsa-miR-200c-3p has been shown to modify TLR4 signaling efficiency dependent on MYD88-mediated pathways in HEK293 cells.
source: Of note, hsa-miR-200c-3p has been shown to modify TLR4 signaling efficiency dependent on MYD88-mediated pathways in an embryonic kidney cell line (HEK293) (Wendlandt et al., 2012).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Wendlandt et al., 2012.

claim: Neutrophil degranulation, protein ubiquitination, and mitotic cell cycle modules correlated with soluble mediators of inflammation, endothelial responses, coagulation, and clinical variables of disease severity.
source: Neutrophil degranulation (secretory; red), protein ubiquitination (pink), and mitotic cell cycle (tan) modules correlated with soluble mediators of inflammation (C reactive protein [CRP], IL-6, IL-10, IL-8), endothelial responses (E-selectin and angiopoietin-2 [ANG2]), coagulation (D-Dimer), and clinical variables of disease severity (Figure 5A).
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis between module eigengenes and clinical/biochemical parameters with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Antigen presentation/Th1-Th2 cell activation, regulation of cytokine secretion/TLR signaling, and type-I interferon signaling/double stranded RNA binding modules were indirectly correlated with various soluble mediators and clinical severity indices.
source: In contrast, antigen presentation/Th1-Th2 cell activation (green module), regulation of cytokine secretion/TLR signaling (black module), and type-I interferon signaling/double stranded RNA binding (salmon module) were indirectly correlated with various soluble mediators and clinical severity indices.
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis between module eigengenes and clinical/biochemical parameters.

claim: Patients with septic shock showed significantly higher neutrophil degranulation (secretory) expression patterns.
source: Patients with septic shock showed significantly higher neutrophil degranulation (secretory) expression patterns (Figure 5B).
evidence: The statement is based on comparison of module eigengene values between shock and no shock patients with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: MYOSLID expression was directly correlated with levels of inflammatory response markers IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, and CRP.
source: In line with their respective module eigengene correlations with inflammatory response markers, MYOSLID expression was directly correlated with levels of inflammatory response markers IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, and acute phase response protein CRP (Figure 5D).
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis between MYOSLID expression and inflammatory markers with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: LUCAT1 expression was indirectly correlated with soluble mediators of inflammation, except for CRP.
source: In contrast, LUCAT1 expression was indirectly correlated with soluble mediators of inflammation, except for CRP (Figure 5E).
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis between LUCAT1 expression and inflammatory markers with reference to Figure 5E.

claim: The study included 156 sepsis patients and 82 healthy subjects.
source: In order to build a comprehensive map of RNA expression in the context of sepsis, we evaluated protein-coding, long and small non-coding RNA expression in whole blood leukocytes from 156 sepsis patients and 82 healthy subjects (median age (Q1–Q3), 54 (42 – 60); 26% male).
evidence: The statement describes the study population size.

claim: Eight healthy volunteers were challenged with lipopolysaccharide in a controlled clinical setting.
source: Here we obtained whole blood from 156 patients with sepsis and 82 healthy subjects among whom eight were challenged with lipopolysaccharide in a clinically controlled setting (human endotoxemia).
evidence: The abstract describes the human endotoxemia experiment.

claim: The median age of sepsis patients was 62 years (Q1-Q3: 50-70).
source: Age, years	62 (50 - 70)
evidence: Table 1 provides demographic data for sepsis patients.

claim: 62.8% of sepsis patients were male.
source: Male sex	98 (62.8)
evidence: Table 1 provides demographic data for sepsis patients.

claim: 89.7% of sepsis patients were of white ethnicity.
source: White ethnicity	140 (89.7)
evidence: Table 1 provides demographic data for sepsis patients.

claim: 75.0% of sepsis patients had medical admission.
source: Medical admission	117 (75.0)
evidence: Table 1 provides clinical characteristics for sepsis patients.

claim: 28.8% of sepsis patients had immune suppression.
source: Immune suppression	45 (28.8)
evidence: Table 1 provides clinical characteristics for sepsis patients.

claim: The median APACHE IV score of sepsis patients was 72 (Q1-Q3: 58-92).
source: APACHE IV score	72 [58 - 92]
evidence: Table 1 provides clinical severity scores for sepsis patients.

claim: The median SOFA score of sepsis patients was 7 (Q1-Q3: 4-9).
source: SOFA score	7 (4 - 9)
evidence: Table 1 provides clinical severity scores for sepsis patients.

claim: 55.1% of sepsis patients had shock.
evidence: Table 1 provides clinical characteristics for sepsis patients.

claim: 82.1% of sepsis patients required mechanical ventilation.
source: Mechanical ventilation	128 (82.1)
evidence: Table 1 provides clinical characteristics for sepsis patients.

claim: 63.5% of sepsis patients had pneumonia as primary diagnosis.
source: Pneumonia	99 (63.5)
evidence: Table 1 provides primary diagnosis data for sepsis patients.

claim: 36.5% of sepsis patients had abdominal sepsis as primary diagnosis.
source: Abdominal sepsis	57 (36.5)
evidence: Table 1 provides primary diagnosis data for sepsis patients.

claim: The 28-day mortality rate was 30.8% in sepsis patients.
source: 28-day mortality	48 (30.8)
evidence: Table 1 provides outcome data for sepsis patients.

claim: The 90-day mortality rate was 37.8% in sepsis patients.
source: 90-day mortality	59 (37.8)
evidence: Table 1 provides outcome data for sepsis patients.

claim: The 1-year mortality rate was 49.4% in sepsis patients.
source: 1-year mortality	77 (49.4)
evidence: Table 1 provides outcome data for sepsis patients.

claim: Sepsis is a multifaceted syndrome that develops as the consequence of an abnormal host response to infection leading to organ failure and high risk of death.
source: Sepsis is a multifaceted syndrome that develops as the consequence of an abnormal host response to infection leading to organ failure and high risk of death (Angus and van der Poll, 2013; Cecconi et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Angus and van der Poll, 2013 and Cecconi et al., 2018.

claim: Lower conservation coupled with faster evolution rates of long non-coding RNA regions may be at the basis of extensive variation in long non-coding RNA expression.
source: Lower conservation coupled with faster evolution rates of long non-coding RNA regions, which seemingly harbor more single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) than protein-coding genes (Necsulea and Kaessmann, 2014), as well as the possibility of their relatively higher susceptibility to environmental and lifestyle factors (Dumeaux et al., 2010), may be at the basis of the extensive variation in long non-coding RNA expression.
evidence: The statement is a speculation based on citations to Necsulea and Kaessmann, 2014 and Dumeaux et al., 2010.

claim: The human endotoxemia model is a highly relevant in vivo model of acute systemic inflammation in the context of a controlled clinical setting.
source: The human endotoxemia model is a highly relevant in vivo model of acute systemic inflammation in the context of a controlled clinical setting (Lowry, 2005).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Lowry, 2005.

claim: The correlation between sepsis and human endotoxemia was dependent on timing of the response to LPS.
source: In extension to the previously reported data, based on a single time-point of human endotoxemia (Seok et al., 2013; Takao and Miyakawa, 2015), we found that the correlation between sepsis and human endotoxemia was also dependent, at least in part, on timing of the response to LPS.
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis at multiple time points and references previous studies.

claim: The highest correlation between sepsis and endotoxemia was found at 4 hr, a time point at which the capacity of cytokine production by leukocytes is typically reduced, indicative of endotoxin tolerance.
source: The highest correlation was found at 4 hr, a time point at which the capacity of cytokine production by leukocytes is typically reduced in the human endotoxemia model, indicative of endotoxin tolerance (Cheng et al., 2016; de Vos et al., 2009).
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis and supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2016 and de Vos et al., 2009.

claim: Small non-coding RNA expression profiles in sepsis patients were not reliably recapitulated in human endotoxemia, primarily showing indirect correlations.
source: In contrast, small non-coding RNA expression profiles in sepsis patients were not reliably recapitulated in human endotoxemia, primarily showing indirect correlations.
evidence: The statement is based on correlation analysis between sepsis and endotoxemia.

claim: Low expression patterns of miRNA compared to protein-coding and long non-coding RNA may explain why small non-coding RNA profiles were not recapitulated in human endotoxemia.
source: This may be due to typically low expression patterns of miRNA, compared to protein-coding and long non-coding RNA, and reported high specificities of miRNA to developmental stage and cell-type (Bernstein et al., 2003).
evidence: The statement is a speculation based on a citation to Bernstein et al., 2003.

claim: The host response during infection is characterized by a balance between resistance and tolerance.
source: The host response during infection is characterized by a balance between resistance (seeking to limit the pathogen load) and tolerance (aiming to retain cell and organ functions) (Schneider and Ayres, 2008).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Schneider and Ayres, 2008.

claim: In sepsis both resistance and tolerance mechanisms can become uncontrolled.
source: In sepsis both mechanisms can become uncontrolled, wherein aberrant activation of resistance pathways results in tissue damage and inadequate tolerance can cause immune suppression with enhanced susceptibility to secondary infections (Bauer and Wetzker, 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Bauer and Wetzker, 2020.

claim: Coding and long non-coding RNA profiles in blood leukocytes of sepsis patients particularly reflect a tolerant state.
source: While our time-sequential data in healthy humans injected with LPS suggest that coding and long non-coding RNA profiles in blood leukocytes of sepsis patients particularly reflect a tolerant state, time course studies in patients are needed to increase the insight into the role of distinct RNA species in the interplay between resistance and tolerance.
evidence: The statement is an inference based on the correlation with the 4-hour endotoxemia time point.

claim: SNPs influencing gene expression patterns were identified in a recent prospective study in sepsis due to community-acquired pneumonia.
source: This was shown in a recent prospective study in sepsis due to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), wherein SNPs influencing gene expression patterns were identified (Davenport et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Davenport et al., 2016.

claim: The time of onset of sepsis cannot be accurately determined, resulting in considerable uncertainty since patients are presumably admitted to the ICU at various stages of the sepsis syndrome.
source: The time of onset of sepsis is a current 'black box' in the field as it cannot be accurately determined, thereby resulting in considerable uncertainty since patients are presumably admitted to the ICU at various stages of the sepsis syndrome.
evidence: The statement is based on knowledge of clinical practice in sepsis.

claim: Cell death or exhaustion, particularly in lymphocytes, have been proposed as causal features of immunosuppression and lethality in sepsis.
source: Cell death or exhaustion, particularly in lymphocytes, have been proposed as causal features of immunosuppression and lethality in sepsis (Hotchkiss et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Hotchkiss et al., 2013.

claim: GABPB1-AS1 is an autophagy and chemical stress responder.
source: Our findings further strengthen this hypothesis and position previously unknown non-coding RNA, including an autophagy and chemical stress responder GABPB1-AS1 (Tani et al., 2014; Luan et al., 2019), as putative regulators of cell death in the context of sepsis.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Tani et al., 2014 and Luan et al., 2019.

claim: Modulation of DNA damage responses was demonstrated as a potential therapeutic path that might be exploited to confer protection to severe sepsis.
source: Modulation of DNA damage responses was demonstrated as a potential therapeutic path that might be exploited to confer protection to severe sepsis (Figueiredo et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Figueiredo et al., 2013.

claim: Olfactory receptors have been shown to be involved in cell–cell recognition, migration, proliferation, and apoptosis.
source: They have been shown to be involved in cell–cell recognition, migration, proliferation, and apoptosis (Maßberg and Hatt, 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Maßberg and Hatt, 2018.

claim: Olfactory receptors are not exclusive to the nose.
source: Little is known about olfactory receptors in non-chemosensory cells, but a growing body of evidence suggests they are not exclusive to the nose (Kang and Koo, 2012).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Kang and Koo, 2012.

claim: The study provides a benchmark dissection of the blood leukocyte 'regulome' that can facilitate prioritization of future functional studies.
source: We provide a benchmark dissection of the blood leukocyte 'regulome' that can facilitate prioritization of future functional studies.
evidence: The abstract states the overall contribution of the study.

claim: The study was part of the Molecular Diagnosis and Risk Stratification of sepsis (MARS) project.
source: This study was part of the Molecular Diagnosis and Risk Stratification of sepsis (MARS) project, a prospective observational study in the mixed ICUs of two tertiary teaching hospitals in the Netherlands (Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam and University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht) (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT01905033) (van Vught et al., 2016a; Klein Klouwenberg et al., 2013; Scicluna et al., 2015b).
evidence: The methods section describes the study design and provides citations.

claim: Total RNA was isolated using PaxGene blood miRNA isolation kit.
source: Total RNA was isolated by means of PaxGene blood miRNA isolation kit (Thermo-Fisher) as per manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: The methods section describes the RNA isolation procedure.

claim: Quality RNA was processed and hybridized to the GeneChip Human Transcriptome Array (HTA) 2.0 or the miRNA 4.1 96-array plate.
source: Quality RNA (Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer, Agilent Technologies; RIN > 6) was processed and hybridized to either the GeneChip Human Transcriptome Array (HTA) 2.0 (Thermo-Fisher) or the miRNA 4.1 96-array plate (Thermo-Fisher) following manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: The methods section describes the microarray procedures.

claim: Microarrays were scanned at the Cologne Center for Genomics, Cologne, Germany.
source: Microarrays were scanned at the Cologne Center for Genomics, Cologne, Germany.
evidence: The methods section describes where microarray scanning was performed.
